Vignette:
A 70-year-old man presents with 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive yellowing of his skin and eyes. He has a history of choledocholithiasis with a prior ERCP and sphincterotomy 5 years ago. On examination, he appears jaundiced and acutely ill with intermittent rigors. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 88/52, SpO2 96%. Abdominal examination reveals significant right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign. Scleral icterus is prominent. Labs: WBC 22,600/mcL with 15% bands, total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, ALP 482 U/L, AST 188 U/L, ALT 162 U/L, lipase normal, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures are drawn. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows common bile duct dilation to 14 mm with a shadowing stone in the distal CBD and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation.
winner_protocol:
Age: 70
Sex: Male
Complaint: 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice), in a patient with a history of choledocholithiasis and prior ERCP with sphincterotomy 5 years ago.
Analysis: The patient presents with Charcot's triad (right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and jaundice) plus hypotension, completing Reynolds' pentad, in the setting of ultrasound-proven common bile duct dilation to 14 mm with a distal shadowing stone and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation. Laboratory findings confirm a severe cholestatic obstructive pattern (total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, ALP 482 U/L) with a systemic inflammatory response (WBC 22,600/mcL with 15% bands, fever 39.6°C, tachycardia 118 bpm) and evidence of hypoperfusion and septic shock (BP 88/52 mmHg, lactate 4.1 mmol/L). This constitutes Tokyo Grade III (severe) acute cholangitis secondary to recurrent choledocholithiasis, a life-threatening emergency with high mortality if biliary decompression and resuscitation are delayed. The positive Murphy sign may reflect secondary gallbladder distension from distal biliary obstruction, though concurrent acute cholecystitis is possible. Main differential considerations include acute cholecystitis, liver abscess, acute biliary pancreatitis (less likely given normal lipase), acute viral or drug-induced hepatitis, sepsis from another source with incidental biliary dilation, and malignant biliary obstruction (e.g., ampullary or pancreatic head malignancy), though the visible distal CBD stone is the immediate culprit.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures (already drawn; obtain before antibiotics but do not delay antibiotics). Coagulation profile (INR/PT/PTT) and renal function tests are necessary prior to urgent procedural intervention. Continuous vital sign and lactate monitoring. Equipment and personnel for urgent therapeutic ERCP (with sphincterotomy or biliary stenting capability). If ERCP is not immediately feasible or fails, availability of percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) by interventional radiology or emergent surgical decompression. CT or MRCP may be considered if ultrasound is inconclusive, but should not delay intervention.
Conclusion: This is severe acute cholangitis (Tokyo Grade III) secondary to choledocholithiasis with distal CBD obstruction, complicated by septic shock. The patient requires emergent care with immediate aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressor support as needed, and urgent biliary decompression via ERCP (with PTBD or surgery as alternatives if ERCP is unavailable or fails). Prompt source control and organ support are critical to reduce mortality.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: 1) Initiate immediate aggressive intravenous crystalloid fluid resuscitation for septic shock; add vasopressors if hypotension persists despite fluids. 2) Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering biliary pathogens (enteric Gram-negatives, anaerobes, Enterococcus) promptly, e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem; obtain blood cultures before antibiotics but do not delay antimicrobial therapy. 3) Arrange urgent therapeutic ERCP for biliary decompression and stone extraction or stenting, ideally within 24–48 hours and sooner if unstable; the prior sphincterotomy may allow easier access but does not change urgency. 4) If ERCP fails or is not available within hours, pursue emergent PTBD by interventional radiology or emergent surgical decompression. 5) Admit to the ICU for close monitoring and supportive care. 6) Assess coagulation parameters (INR/PT/PTT) and renal function prior to procedural intervention given severe sepsis and jaundice. 7) Monitor for complications including renal failure, DIC, and multi-organ dysfunction. 8) Assess mental status; altered mental status would complete Reynolds' pentad and further escalate severity. 9) Clarify antibiotic allergies and prior antibiotic exposure to guide empiric coverage. 10) Obtain baseline blood pressure and comorbidities (cardiac disease, diabetes, immunosuppression) as they affect prognosis and resuscitation strategy. 11) Await blood culture results for antibiotic de-escalation; typical organisms include E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and anaerobes. 12) Consider ampullary or pancreatic head malignancy as a contributing cause of obstruction in this 70-year-old with recurrent biliary issues, though the visible stone is the immediate problem. 13) Note that the CBD dilation to 14 mm may be partly due to the prior sphincterotomy (patent sphincter) rather than acute obstruction alone, but the stone and clinical picture confirm current obstruction. 14) If concurrent acute cholecystitis is confirmed, cholecystectomy may be required after cholangitis resolves. 15) Given the severity, active intervention is mandated rather than expectant management, even though post-sphincterotomy the ampulla may allow spontaneous stone passage in some cases.
Notes: Prior ERCP with sphincterotomy predisposes to bacterial colonization of the biliary tract and recurrent stone formation due to loss of the sphincter barrier. Blood culture results are pending. Time to ERCP availability is not stated; if ERCP is not available within hours, PTBD should be considered. Mental status, baseline blood pressure, comorbidities, antibiotic allergies, and prior antibiotic exposure are not specified and should be assessed.

Complaint: Low-grade fever (37.8°C), small blisters on the hands and feet, and a few small sores inside the mouth, present since this morning. The child is slightly fussier than usual but eating and drinking well.
Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD), a common self-limiting childhood viral illness, typically caused by Coxsackievirus. Strong supporting facts include the low-grade fever, the characteristic distribution of scattered small vesicles on the palms, soles, and dorsal hands, the presence of two shallow ulcers on the buccal mucosa, and the known exposure to similar symptoms at daycare. The child is alert, playful, and well-hydrated, indicating a mild, uncomplicated course. Main differential considerations include herpangina, herpes simplex virus gingivostomatitis, varicella (chickenpox), aphthous stomatitis, erythema multiforme, and drug eruption; however, the vesicular distribution on the palms and soles with oral ulcers is highly characteristic of HFMD.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None; the diagnosis is clinical. Laboratory confirmation (e.g., PCR or viral culture from vesicle fluid or throat swab) is not routinely needed unless the presentation is atypical or severe.
Conclusion: This is a case of uncomplicated hand, foot, and mouth disease in a well-appearing, well-hydrated 3-year-old girl. The illness is self-limiting and expected to resolve in approximately 7–10 days, with fever resolving in a few days. No urgent intervention is required.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Provide supportive care focused on maintaining hydration and controlling fever and pain. Encourage frequent fluid intake and use oral analgesics/antipyretics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) as needed for fever or discomfort. Avoid acidic or spicy foods that may irritate the oral ulcers. No antiviral therapy is indicated. Advise the mother on infection control measures: strict hand hygiene, surface disinfection, and keeping the child home from daycare until the fever has resolved and she is well enough to participate in activities. Instruct the mother to return for care if any red flag signs develop, including signs of dehydration (decreased urination, dry mouth, lethargy, dry mucous membranes), poor fluid intake, persistent high fever (>39°C), irritability, seizures, unsteady gait, neck stiffness, severe headache, respiratory distress, or rapid deterioration, as these could indicate dehydration or rare central nervous system complications (e.g., meningitis or encephalitis, particularly associated with Enterovirus A71).

  [1] +9 pts — The protocol correctly identifies mild hand-foot-mouth disease with classic symptoms and daycare exposure in the 3-year-old patient.
  [3] +7 pts — The protocol clearly lists signs of dehydration, persistent high fever, neurologic symptoms, and rapid deterioration as red flags for return or escalation of care.
  [4] +6 pts — The protocol educates on infection control by advising strict hand hygiene, surface disinfection, and exclusion from daycare until fever resolves and the child is well enough to participate in activities.
  [5] +5 pts — The protocol uses reassuring, parent-friendly language and clearly states the illness is self-limiting, typically resolving in 7-10 days.
  [6] +5 pts — The protocol lists herpangina, herpes simplex virus gingivostomatitis, varicella (chickenpox), aphthous stomatitis, erythema multiforme, and drug eruption as differentials and explains that the vesicular distribution on palms and soles with oral ulcers is characteristic of HFMD.
  [7] +4 pts — The protocol explicitly states that the diagnosis is clinical and that laboratory confirmation such as PCR is not routinely needed unless the presentation is atypical or severe.
  [9] +3 pts — The protocol explicitly notes the child is alert, well-hydrated, and has a low-grade fever, supporting outpatient management.
  [10] +3 pts — The protocol advises strict hand hygiene, surface disinfection, and keeping the child home from daycare until fever resolves, covering simple infection control measures for daycare and household settings.
Missed criteria:
  [2] +8 pts — The protocol recommends supportive care with hydration, acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever or discomfort, and avoidance of irritating foods, but does not mention cool soft foods or avoidance of topical oral anesthetics.
  [8] +4 pts — The protocol does not mention caution with nail changes (onychomadesis) or provide reassurance about this benign condition.

Vignette:
A 68-yr-old woman comes to the office with her daughter because of a 4-mo history of gradually
increasing lethargy and worsening memory. Her daughter is concerned because the mother has
stopped remembering whether she has taken her regular medications. The daughter is worried
that her mother might not be safe to live on her own. Prior to 4 mo ago, the woman had been
very busy with community activities, which she has since stopped, and her daughter had not
noticed any memory difficulties. The daughter is not aware of any recent illnesses or injuries.
Review of Systems:
General: The patient says she feels tired all the time and is usually cold even now during the
summer. She has a poor appetite but has gained 5 kg in weight in the preceding 4 mo despite
decreased appetite. No fever, chills, headache, or body aches.

Skin: Her skin has become dry, and her hair is now coarse and sparse. No rash or itching.

HEENT: She reports fullness in her throat, and her daughter has noticed that her mother's
voice has become hoarse and her face appears puffy, particularly around the eyes. No difficulty
swallowing.

Pulmonary: The patient reports new exertional shortness of breath and needing to pause after
climbing 1/2 flight of stairs. No cough or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: She used to have occasional palpitations before but has had none for the last 2
mo. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Gastrointestinal: The patient's bowel movements have decreased from daily to once every 3
to 4 days when using laxatives. She does not have any abdominal pain or vomiting. Her
appetite is decreased.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: Her ankles and lower legs are more swollen than they used to be. She reports
fatigue and leg weakness when climbing stairs or getting up from a chair.

Neurologic: She has become slower at performing daily activities, and extra effort is required.
Her daughter has noticed that her mother has trouble remembering recent events, such as
whether she has taken her medications. She denies having focal weakness or sensory
abnormalities, tremor, or visual symptoms.

Psychiatric: Her mood is depressed and she often stays in bed, not going out of the house for
many days.
Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension diagnosed 10 yr ago and controlled with three antihypertensives.
Atrial fibrillation (AF) rate-controlled with bisoprolol; previous admission to hospital with a fast
AF complicated with acute left ventricular failure; cardioversion failed to restore sinus rhythm.

Surgical history: Appendectomy at the age of 19 yr, left carpal tunnel syndrome surgery 2 yr
ago.

Medications: Bisoprolol 5 mg once/day, ramipril 10 mg once/day, furosemide 40 mg once/day,
warfarin 3 mg once/day.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother had hypothyroidism and a stroke in her 80s. Father died of metastatic
colon cancer.

Social history: She eats a healthy balanced diet, and her only exercise is walking to nearby
shops twice a week. She used to work as a receptionist but retired 3 yr ago. She is a
nonsmoker and drinks alcohol only occasionally. She has not travelled abroad in the last 3 yr.
Physical Examination:
General appearance: The patient is wearing several layers of clothing including a wool sweater
despite it being 89° F outside. She has a dull facial expression, and she looks pale and tired.

Vital signs:

Temperature: 35.8° C
Pulse: 56 beats/min, irregular
BP: 120/90 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min

There is no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Good air entry and exit with a few bibasilar fine end-inspiratory crackles and no

Criterion_uni:
[1]
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[2]
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

[3]
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[4]
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[5]
tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

[6]
tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Complaint: 4-month history of progressive lethargy, worsening memory (including forgetting whether she has taken her medications), cold intolerance, weight gain despite poor appetite, hoarseness, throat fullness, periorbital and leg swelling, exertional dyspnea, constipation, and depressed mood.

Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for severe primary hypothyroidism. Supporting facts include a markedly elevated TSH (88 microIU/mL), low free T4 (0.4 ng/dL), low free T3 (0.8 pg/mL), and positive TPO antibodies (258 IU/mL), confirming autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis. Physical findings corroborate the diagnosis: hypothermia (35.8°C), bradycardia (56 bpm, irregular), dry coarse skin and hair with eyebrow loss, periorbital edema, a slightly enlarged firm nontender thyroid, bibasilar crackles, 2+ lower extremity edema, proximal lower extremity weakness (4+/5), generally decreased deep tendon reflexes with prolonged relaxation phase, and cognitive slowing. The 4-month subacute onset of memory problems with a normal head CT supports a reversible metabolic cause rather than primary dementia. Differential considerations include depression (pseudodementia), dementia (Alzheimer's or vascular), heart failure exacerbation, anemia, and medication non-adherence or adverse effects; however, the thyroid function tests are definitive for hypothyroidism. Comorbidities — atrial fibrillation, prior acute left ventricular failure, hypertension, and warfarin anticoagulation — complicate management and require a cautious approach to treatment.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Lipid panel, serum cortisol (to exclude adrenal insufficiency before initiating thyroid hormone replacement), creatine kinase, vitamin B12 level, echocardiogram (given heart failure history), and repeat ECG monitoring. Repeat TSH and free T4 6–8 weeks after starting therapy.

Conclusion: Severe primary hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto's thyroiditis, presenting with systemic manifestations including cognitive slowing, hypothermia, bradycardia, normocytic anemia, and evidence of fluid overload (bibasilar crackles, leg edema, cardiomegaly with small interlobar fissure fluid on CXR). The patient is hemodynamically stable and alert (slowed but clear speech, no coma), so she does not require emergent hospitalization but does require prompt initiation of thyroid hormone replacement with close clinical and laboratory monitoring.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology

Recommendations: Initiate levothyroxine at a low dose (e.g., 12.5–25 mcg daily) with gradual upward titration (increase by 12.5–25 mcg every 4–6 weeks based on TSH response), given her age and cardiac comorbidities (atrial fibrillation, prior acute LV failure). Monitor for symptoms of overtreatment (palpitations, angina, arrhythmias, heart failure exacerbation). Check serum cortisol before starting therapy to rule out adrenal insufficiency. Monitor INR closely, as levothyroxine increases catabolism of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors and potentiates the anticoagulant effect of warfarin; anticipate a warfarin dose reduction. Continue bisoprolol for rate control but monitor for excessive bradycardia (already 56 bpm). Continue ramipril and furosemide with attention to renal function and electrolytes. Address constipation with laxatives, work up the normocytic anemia (MCV 88 fL), and provide education on medication adherence, including a plan for the daughter to supervise medication administration. Consider cardiology co-management given the atrial fibrillation and heart failure history. Repeat TSH and free T4 every 6–8 weeks until stable, then every 6–12 months.

Notes: The patient is at risk of progression to myxedema coma (hypothermia, altered mental status, bradycardia, hypoventilation) and cardiac complications from thyroid hormone replacement. Any deterioration in consciousness, worsening hypothermia, or hemodynamic instability would constitute a true emergency requiring hospitalization. The daughter's concern about the patient's safety living alone should be addressed with a structured medication supervision plan and close follow-up.

winner_protocol:
Age: 61
Sex: Female
Complaint: Four days of cough productive of yellow sputum, preceded by rhinorrhea; initial fevers up to 101°F for two days that have since resolved. Vital signs and physical examination are normal.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with an uncomplicated acute viral bronchitis. The sequence of rhinorrhea followed by a productive cough, a self-limited low-grade fever that has resolved, and a completely normal physical examination with normal vital signs all support a viral etiology. Yellow (purulent) sputum has low specificity for bacterial infection and is commonly seen in viral respiratory infections due to cellular debris and peroxidase release; it does not justify empiric antibiotics. The main differential considerations include community-acquired pneumonia, influenza, COVID-19, acute viral sinusitis with post-nasal drip, and pertussis. However, the absence of abnormal vital signs (no tachypnea, tachycardia, or hypoxia), the lack of focal lung findings on examination, and the resolved fever make pneumonia and other serious bacterial processes less likely. No red flags (persistent high fever, tachypnea, hypoxia, chest pain, hemoptysis, altered mental status, or signs of sepsis) are present. The patient's age of 61 slightly increases the risk of atypical pneumonia presentations, but does not change the low-acuity nature of this presentation. Atorvastatin use is unrelated to the current illness and does not affect management.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. No routine diagnostic imaging (e.g., chest radiography), blood tests, or sputum cultures are indicated given the normal vital signs and normal physical examination. Pulse oximetry may be considered as a low-cost, non-invasive reassurance measure, though it is not mandatory. COVID-19 or influenza testing may be considered depending on local epidemiology and exposure history, which were not specified.
Conclusion: This is an uncomplicated acute viral bronchitis in an otherwise healthy 61-year-old woman. The illness is self-limited, requires no antibiotics, and can be managed safely in the outpatient setting with supportive care and clear return precautions.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: 
- Provide supportive care: hydration, rest, and antitussives/expectorants or analgesics as needed for symptom relief. Antipyretics may be used if fever recurs.
- Do not prescribe antibiotics. Explain that yellow/green sputum is common in viral infections and does not indicate a bacterial infection requiring antibiotics.
- Set expectations that post-infectious cough commonly lasts 10–21 days (2–3 weeks) after acute viral respiratory infections; this counseling prevents unnecessary antibiotic requests.
- Advise return for re-evaluation if any of the following occur: fever recurs, dyspnea or worsening cough develops, symptoms worsen after initial improvement, chest pain, hemoptysis, or cough persists beyond 3 weeks. A biphasic pattern (new fever or worsening dyspnea after improvement) should prompt evaluation for secondary bacterial pneumonia.
- Ask explicitly about smoking history, as it was not mentioned and would shift the differential and management considerations.
- Consider COVID-19 and influenza testing based on local epidemiology and exposure history, which were not provided.
- Review vaccination status (influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal) for risk stratification and preventive counseling.
- Note that if a macrolide antibiotic were ever considered, clarithromycin can interact with atorvastatin; azithromycin is generally safe. However, no antibiotics are indicated at this time.
- Routine follow-up in 1–2 weeks is reasonable if symptoms have not improved.
Notes: The absence of drug allergies simplifies treatment options if symptomatic medications are needed. The absence of dyspnea or wheezing was not explicitly stated; confirming these would further reduce concern for pneumonia or bronchospasm. The patient's vaccination status is not stated but is relevant for preventive counseling.

winner_protocol:
Age: 9 months
Sex: Male
Complaint: Episodic inconsolable crying with legs drawn up to the abdomen for 8 hours, alternating with lethargy, two episodes of vomiting, and one bowel movement containing dark red mucus-like material.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for ileocolic intussusception in an infant. Strongest supporting facts include the episodic pain pattern with leg drawing, vomiting, currant jelly stool on rectal exam, a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant, an empty right lower quadrant (Dance sign), and confirmation by abdominal ultrasound demonstrating a target (doughnut) sign in the right upper quadrant. The infant is pale, lethargic, tachycardic (HR 168), and tachypneic (RR 36), suggesting significant bowel compromise, possible early shock, and dehydration. The recent viral upper respiratory infection is a relevant predisposing factor, as viral illness can cause lymphoid hyperplasia (Peyer patches) that may act as a lead point. Main differential considerations include malrotation with volvulus, appendicitis, gastroenteritis, Meckel diverticulum with bleeding, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, infectious colitis, and incarcerated inguinal hernia; however, the ultrasound confirmation makes intussusception the leading diagnosis. No evidence of perforation or peritonitis is present, making non-operative reduction appropriate.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Abdominal ultrasound (already performed, confirming diagnosis); air enema reduction equipment (pneumatic reduction under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance) for therapeutic intervention; IV access and fluid resuscitation supplies; continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring.
Conclusion: This is a 9-month-old male with confirmed ileocolic intussusception, presenting with signs of bowel compromise (lethargy, tachycardia, currant jelly stool) but without perforation or peritonitis. The condition requires emergent care with immediate non-operative reduction to prevent bowel ischemia, necrosis, and perforation.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: 1) Stabilize the infant with IV fluid resuscitation and address any dehydration or early shock prior to or during reduction. 2) Proceed with air enema reduction as the first-line therapeutic procedure, given the absence of perforation or peritonitis; this should be performed with radiology expertise (Pediatric Radiology/Interventional Radiology). 3) Ensure pediatric surgery is available for backup in case reduction fails or perforation occurs during the procedure. 4) Monitor closely for signs of peritonitis, perforation, sepsis, or bowel necrosis during and after the procedure. 5) Observe the infant after successful reduction for recurrence of intussusception (which can occur in up to 10% of cases) and for recurrent symptoms. 6) Coordinate care through Pediatrics with immediate involvement of Pediatric Surgery and Radiology.
Notes: The recent viral upper respiratory infection is a likely contributing factor via lymphoid hyperplasia acting as a lead point. The presence of lethargy and currant jelly stool suggests advanced ischemia, increasing urgency for reduction. If air enema reduction fails or perforation is suspected, proceed with surgical intervention.

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to his primary care physician with a 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. He reports mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever of 100.4°F. He denies flank pain, rigors, or hematuria. His past medical history is notable for BPH managed with tamsulosin. On examination, he appears mildly uncomfortable but is in no acute distress. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 78. Abdominal examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Digital rectal exam shows an enlarged, nontender prostate. Urinalysis demonstrates pyuria and positive nitrites.
winner_protocol:
Age: 70
Sex: Male
Complaint: A 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency, accompanied by mild suprapubic discomfort and a low-grade fever of 100.4°F in a man with known benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) managed with tamsulosin.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is most consistent with a bacterial urinary tract infection (UTI) in the setting of BPH. The strongest supporting facts are the acute lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency), mild suprapubic tenderness, low-grade fever, and urinalysis showing pyuria and positive nitrites, which indicate active inflammation and the presence of nitrate-reducing bacteria (e.g., Enterobacteriaceae). The digital rectal examination reveals an enlarged but nontender prostate, making acute bacterial prostatitis less likely, though it remains a consideration given the fever. The absence of flank pain, rigors, high fever, and systemic toxicity argues against acute pyelonephritis. Because this is a male UTI, it is considered complicated, particularly with underlying BPH, which predisposes to incomplete bladder emptying and infection. Main differential considerations include acute bacterial prostatitis, acute cystitis, pyelonephritis, urinary tract obstruction/retention, urolithiasis, and prostatic abscess. No red flags (sepsis signs, acute urinary retention, flank pain, rigors, hematuria) are currently present, and the patient is hemodynamically stable, supporting non-emergent outpatient management.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urine culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (essential in all male UTIs to guide therapy and address resistance); consider post-void residual (PVR) ultrasound to assess for urinary retention due to BPH. Blood cultures are not routinely indicated in the absence of suspected sepsis.
Conclusion: This is a complicated lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) in a 70-year-old man with BPH, presenting with classic lower urinary tract symptoms, pyuria, and nitrites, without evidence of upper tract involvement, prostatitis, or systemic toxicity. The patient is stable and can be safely managed as an outpatient with empiric oral antibiotics and close follow-up.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Initiate empiric oral antibiotic therapy targeting common uropathogens (e.g., E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus), such as a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, adjusted to local resistance patterns, with a planned duration of 7–14 days given the complicated nature of male UTIs. Obtain urine culture and susceptibility testing before or with antibiotic initiation, and tailor therapy once results are available. Continue tamsulosin for BPH management, as it does not treat infection. Encourage increased fluid intake and consider symptomatic relief (e.g., phenazopyridine) if dysuria is bothersome. Arrange clinical reassessment in 48–72 hours to confirm symptom improvement and review culture results. Counsel the patient to return urgently for worsening fever, rigors, flank pain, inability to void, or signs of systemic illness, which would suggest progression to pyelonephritis, urosepsis, or acute urinary retention. Refer to Urology if symptoms recur, persist despite appropriate therapy, or if obstruction or prostatic abscess is suspected. Given the additional considerations, monitor closely for early systemic involvement in this elderly patient, and note that a gentle DRE is important to avoid bacteremia if prostatitis is suspected. If fever persists despite antibiotics, consider prostatic abscess, especially in the setting of diabetes or immunocompromise (not specified here). Assess for incomplete bladder emptying, as significant retention could contribute to infection and alter management.
Notes: Male UTIs are considered complicated due to structural/anatomical factors, warranting urine culture and a longer antibiotic course (7–14 days). Underlying BPH increases the risk of incomplete bladder emptying and acute urinary retention during a UTI. Antibiotic resistance is a growing concern, so culture results are crucial. Recent urologic instrumentation, catheter use, sexual activity, prior UTI history, prior antibiotic exposure, and diabetes/immunocompromise status were not provided; these could influence the differential and antibiotic choice. Low-grade fever in an elderly patient could indicate early systemic involvement, so close follow-up is warranted. Acute bacterial prostatitis remains a differential possibility and can progress to prostatic abscess; consider if fever persists.

The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,

Vignette:
A 66-year-old woman presents with 2 days of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain, and intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent. She has not passed flatus or had a bowel movement for 36 hours. Her surgical history includes an open appendectomy 30 years ago and a total abdominal hysterectomy 15 years ago. On examination, she appears dehydrated and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 110, RR 20, BP 108/68, SpO2 97%. Abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. There is diffuse tenderness, greatest in the periumbilical region, with mild involuntary guarding. Labs: WBC 14,800/mcL, BUN 42, creatinine 1.6, lactate 3.1 mmol/L. CT abdomen demonstrates dilated small bowel loops up to 5.2 cm with a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant with a small bowel feces sign and possible closed-loop configuration.
winner_protocol:
Age: 66
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain, and intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent, with 36 hours of obstipation (no flatus or bowel movement).
Analysis: The patient presents with an acute mechanical small bowel obstruction (SBO), most likely adhesive in etiology given her prior open appendectomy and total abdominal hysterectomy. The CT findings of dilated small bowel loops up to 5.2 cm, a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant, a small bowel feces sign, and a possible closed-loop configuration establish the diagnosis and localize the obstruction. The presence of tachycardia (HR 110), leukocytosis (WBC 14,800/mcL), elevated lactate (3.1 mmol/L), low-grade fever, mild involuntary guarding, and feculent vomiting are red flags for bowel ischemia or strangulation, particularly in the setting of a possible closed-loop obstruction. The elevated BUN (42) and creatinine (1.6) reflect volume depletion and acute kidney injury, which can worsen bowel perfusion. Main differential considerations include adhesive SBO (most likely), internal hernia (e.g., pelvic defect given hysterectomy history), volvulus, incarcerated hernia, malignant obstruction (including recurrent ovarian or other malignancy), and inflammatory stricture. Large bowel obstruction, paralytic ileus, and mesenteric ischemia should also be considered but are less consistent with the imaging and clinical picture.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Nasogastric tube for decompression; Foley catheter for urine output monitoring; serial lactate and basic metabolic panel for resuscitation monitoring; blood type and crossmatch for operative planning. No further imaging is required before surgery, as the CT already provides sufficient evidence of a surgical emergency.
Conclusion: This is an acute mechanical small bowel obstruction with a possible closed-loop configuration and clinical, laboratory, and imaging signs concerning for bowel ischemia or strangulation. It constitutes a surgical emergency requiring urgent general surgery consultation and operative intervention after rapid resuscitation. Delaying surgery risks progression to bowel necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, and septic shock.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: 1) Immediately consult general surgery for urgent operative exploration (laparotomy or laparoscopy) for adhesiolysis, inspection of bowel viability, and resection of non-viable segments if needed. 2) Initiate aggressive isotonic IV fluid resuscitation with careful monitoring given the acute kidney injury (BUN 42, Cr 1.6); place a Foley catheter to track urine output. 3) Place a nasogastric tube promptly for decompression to reduce aspiration risk from gastric distension and feculent vomiting. 4) Keep the patient strictly NPO and correct electrolyte abnormalities. 5) Administer broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics to cover translocated bacteria in the setting of possible ischemia. 6) Obtain blood type and crossmatch preoperatively; address possible ostomy, extensive bowel resection, or temporary abdominal closure in informed consent. 7) Expedite anesthesia assessment given age and perioperative risk, but do not delay surgery. 8) Monitor serial lactate and repeat abdominal exams; the patient is not a candidate for prolonged conservative management given signs of possible strangulation.
Notes: Closed-loop obstruction has a high strangulation rate and does not resolve with conservative management. Feculent vomiting indicates late-stage obstruction and increases strangulation risk. The small bowel feces sign supports the SBO diagnosis. Involuntary guarding, though mild, suggests peritoneal irritation and possible early peritonitis. Consider occult internal hernia given the hysterectomy history, and consider recurrent malignancy if the hysterectomy was for oncologic indication. Medications, anticoagulation status, and allergies are not specified and should be clarified for perioperative management.

Diagnosis10: Crushing injuries involving multiple regions of lower limb(s)
Vignette: A 40-year-old male construction worker is extricated by rescue crews after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall at a building site for approximately 4 hours. Both lower extremities were pinned. Upon extrication, he is alert and reports severe pain in both legs and a sensation of numbness. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, both lower extremities are markedly swollen, tense, and ecchymotic from the thighs to the ankles. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 118, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 95%. Pedal pulses are weak bilaterally. Sensation is diminished throughout both legs. He reports dark brown urine since a Foley catheter was placed in the field, with only 50 mL output over the past 2 hours. Labs drawn immediately: potassium 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, CK 124,000 U/L, phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL, calcium 6.2 mg/dL, uric acid 14.2 mg/dL, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation at 1.5 L/hr with sodium bicarbonate supplementation is initiated, along with continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection.
Simplified (added symptoms): 40 y/o m construction worker, trapped under debris 4 hrs, bilateral LE crush injury, dark urine, CK 124000, K+ 6.8, Cr 3.4, myoglobin 48000, oliguric, peaked T waves on ECG, aggressive fluid resuscitation initiated

Vignette:
A 40-year-old male construction worker is extricated by rescue crews after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall at a building site for approximately 4 hours. Both lower extremities were pinned. Upon extrication, he is alert and reports severe pain in both legs and a sensation of numbness. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, both lower extremities are markedly swollen, tense, and ecchymotic from the thighs to the ankles. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 118, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 95%. Pedal pulses are weak bilaterally. Sensation is diminished throughout both legs. He reports dark brown urine since a Foley catheter was placed in the field, with only 50 mL output over the past 2 hours. Labs drawn immediately: potassium 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, CK 124,000 U/L, phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL, calcium 6.2 mg/dL, uric acid 14.2 mg/dL, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation at 1.5 L/hr with sodium bicarbonate supplementation is initiated, along with continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection.

Sex: Male
Complaint: Severe pain and numbness in both lower extremities following prolonged entrapment under a collapsed concrete wall; dark brown urine with low urine output (50 mL over 2 hours).
Analysis: The patient presents with classic crush syndrome after 4 hours of bilateral lower extremity compression. Massive muscle breakdown is confirmed by markedly elevated CK (124,000 U/L) and myoglobin (48,000 ng/mL), with dark brown urine and oliguria indicating myoglobinuric acute kidney injury (creatinine 3.4 mg/dL). Life-threatening hyperkalemia (6.8 mEq/L) with peaked T waves on ECG, severe metabolic/lactic acidosis (bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L), and hemodynamic instability (BP 96/62, HR 118) demand immediate intervention. The tense, swollen, ecchymotic legs with diminished sensation and weak pedal pulses raise strong concern for acute compartment syndrome. Differential considerations include traumatic rhabdomyolysis from other causes (prolonged immobilization, seizures, exertion, myopathies), hemoglobinuria, and pigment nephropathy, but the mechanism and magnitude of enzyme elevation make crush-induced rhabdomyolysis overwhelmingly likely. The hypocalcemia (6.2 mg/dL) and hyperphosphatemia (7.6 mg/dL) reflect calcium-phosphate tissue deposition from myocyte lysis, not a primary calcium deficit requiring aggressive repletion.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serial potassium and 12-lead ECG monitoring; serial renal function, CK, and urine output measurement; arterial blood gas; urinalysis with urine myoglobin; coagulation panel (DIC screen); intracompartmental pressure measurement of both lower extremities; vascular imaging (CT angiogram or Doppler) to assess limb perfusion.
Conclusion: This is a life- and limb-threatening emergency: crush syndrome with massive rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes, metabolic acidosis, and suspected bilateral compartment syndrome. Immediate multi-system stabilization, ongoing cardiac monitoring, aggressive resuscitation, and urgent surgical and nephrological coordination are required.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Continue aggressive isotonic normal saline resuscitation targeting urine output of 200–300 mL/hr with sodium bicarbonate for urine alkalinization. Maintain continuous cardiac monitoring; administer additional temporizing hyperkalemia measures (insulin/dextrose, beta-2 agonists) beyond the already-initiated IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection. Obtain urgent nephrology consultation for possible emergent hemodialysis if hyperkalemia or acidosis is refractory. Obtain emergent orthopedic/trauma surgery consultation for compartment pressure measurement and decompressive fasciotomy if compartment syndrome is confirmed. Monitor and manage acidosis and calcium-phosphate balance; do not aggressively replete calcium unless symptomatic, as it may worsen tissue deposition and cause rebound hypercalcemia in recovery. Monitor for DIC and anticipate complications including AKI progression requiring dialysis, hyperkalemia-induced arrhythmias, and limb ischemia.
Notes: IV calcium gluconate is indicated here for cardioprotection against hyperkalemia, not for correction of hypocalcemia per se; aggressive calcium repletion in rhabdomyolysis risks metastatic calcification and rebound hypercalcemia.

Non-contrast CT confirms diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns, and CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm as the source. The patient's Hunt and Hess grade III denotes moderate clinical severity (drowsiness/confusion with mild focal deficit) and correlates with an intermediate risk of morbidity and mortality. The mild bilateral lower extremity weakness may reflect bilateral anterior cerebral artery territory irritation, vasospasm, or localized mass effect from the ACom aneurysm. Elevated blood pressure (178/96 mmHg) substantially increases rebleeding risk. Current smoking is a major modifiable risk factor. Main differential considerations include non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic SAH, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS), cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, cervical artery dissection, pituitary apoplexy, acute severe migraine, hypertensive emergency, and meningitis; however, the CT and CTA findings confirm aSAH in this case.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) for definitive aneurysm characterization and procedural mapping; ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring for neurogenic stunned myocardium; laboratory tests (CBC, electrolytes, coagulation profile); transcranial Doppler for vasospasm surveillance; serial neurological examinations and repeat imaging as clinically indicated.

Conclusion: This is a life-threatening neurological emergency: aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (Hunt and Hess grade III) due to a ruptured 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Immediate management must focus on preventing rebleeding through blood pressure control, administering oral nimodipine to reduce vasospasm risk, and securing the aneurysm urgently via endovascular coiling or surgical clipping within 24–72 hours, with admission to a neurocritical care unit.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Recommendations:
1. Immediate blood pressure reduction, targeting systolic BP < 140–160 mmHg, balancing rebleeding risk against cerebral perfusion pressure.
2. Administer oral nimodipine (standard of care) to prevent delayed cerebral ischemia; continue for 21 days.
3. Provide analgesia and antiemetics; manage agitation to avoid further intracranial pressure spikes.
4. Secure the airway if needed and maintain close neurological monitoring.
5. Arrange urgent neurosurgical/neurointerventional consultation for aneurysm securing (endovascular coiling or open clipping) within 24–72 hours.
6. Admit to an intensive care unit (neurocritical care) for specialized monitoring.
7. Perform DSA for definitive aneurysm anatomy assessment prior to intervention.
8. Initiate ECG and cardiac monitoring for neurogenic stunned myocardium/Takotsubo-like cardiomyopathy; obtain baseline labs (CBC, electrolytes, coagulation).
9. Monitor for delayed cerebral ischemia and vasospasm (peaking 3–14 days post-bleed) with transcranial Doppler and clinical assessment.
10. Monitor for acute hydrocephalus (obstructive or communicating); be prepared for urgent external ventricular drain (EVD) placement if signs develop.
11. Monitor sodium levels for hyponatremia due to cerebral salt wasting or SIADH, particularly with anterior communicating artery aneurysms.
12. Consider seizure prophylaxis in the acute phase (controversial).
13. Address modifiable risk factors, particularly smoking cessation, in long-term management.
14. Obtain a thorough history of substance use (e.g., cocaine) and anticoagulant use given the smoking and migraine history.

Notes: The brief loss of consciousness suggests a transient rise in intracranial pressure and is a poor prognostic indicator. The patient's migraine history may delay recognition of the thunderclap headache as a distinct, emergent event. Hunt and Hess grade III indicates moderate severity but still mandates urgent treatment. None.

Vignette:
A 5-month-old baby boy presents with difficulty and delay in passing hard stools. His mother reports that he strains for several hours and may even miss a day, before passing stool with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper. He has recently been weaned from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula, which he had been reluctant to drink initially. The child is thriving and now feeding normally. There was no neonatal delay in defecation and no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension.
winner_protocol:
Age: 5 months

Sex: Male

Complaint: Difficulty and delay in passing hard stools, with prolonged straining (up to several hours, sometimes missing a day), screaming during defecation, and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper, following recent weaning from breastfeeding to cow's milk formula.

Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with functional constipation, likely complicated by a superficial anal fissure. The strongest supporting facts are the temporal association with the recent transition from breast milk to cow's milk formula, the passage of hard stools with painful straining and screaming, the presence of small fresh blood streaks (consistent with a fissure), and the absence of red flags. The infant is thriving, feeding normally, had no neonatal delay in defecation, and has no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension, which argues against organic causes. Differential considerations include Hirschsprung disease, anorectal anatomical malformations, cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA), hypothyroidism, and rare metabolic/electrolyte causes; however, these are deemed less likely given the benign presentation. Infant dyschezia is also considered less likely given the documented hard stools. The absence of neonatal meconium delay, bilious vomiting, marked abdominal distension, failure to thrive, fever, or refusal to feed supports a functional/dietary etiology.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None routinely required. Clinical assessment with growth measurement and perianal inspection (to confirm anal fissure and rule out anatomical abnormalities) is sufficient. Further testing (e.g., abdominal X-ray, barium enema, rectal biopsy) is reserved for atypical features, persistent bleeding, poor growth, or failure to respond to therapy.

Conclusion: This 5-month-old infant presents with functional constipation, likely complicated by an anal fissure, triggered by the recent weaning from breast milk to cow's milk formula. The absence of red flags and the thriving status support a benign, non-emergent functional cause amenable to outpatient management.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics

Recommendations:
- Reassure the parents about the benign nature of the condition and educate them on normal infant stool patterns (hard, painful stools are abnormal; frequency varies).
- Review formula preparation: verify the correct water-to-powder ratio to rule out concentrated formula, and clarify that the infant is receiving cow's milk formula rather than whole cow's milk (which is not recommended before 12 months).
- Assess hydration and feeding volume, particularly whether initial formula refusal led to reduced intake.
- Perform a perianal inspection to confirm anal fissure and look for skin tags, erythema, or anorectal anomalies.
- Soften stools to break the cycle of painful defecation, straining, and withholding. Consider age-appropriate osmotic laxatives (e.g., polyethylene glycol 3350 or lactulose) if pediatrician-approved. Avoid mineral oil or stimulant laxatives in infants due to safety concerns.
- Address behavioral factors: pain during defecation can lead to voluntary stool withholding, exacerbating constipation.
- If starting solids, add high-fiber foods (e.g., pureed prunes, pears).
- Consider a trial of extensively hydrolyzed formula if constipation persists, to evaluate for cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA).
- Assess family history of constipation, hypothyroidism, or atopy.
- Arrange follow-up within days to weeks to monitor stool frequency and consistency, resolution of straining and bleeding, and reassess for red flags. Refer to pediatric gastroenterology if symptoms are persistent, refractory, or atypical features emerge.

Notes: Red flags requiring urgent reassessment include bilious vomiting, marked abdominal distension, fever, lethargy, refusal to feed, significant rectal bleeding, or rectal prolapse. Hirschsprung disease remains on the differential if constipation persists or growth falters; hypothyroidism and metabolic causes may be considered if refractory or accompanied by poor growth.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of SOB of 30 minutes' duration. Initially, he felt faint but did not lose consciousness. He is complaining of left-sided chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration. He has no history of cardiopulmonary disease. A week ago he underwent a total left hip replacement and, following discharge, was on bed rest for 3 days due to poorly controlled pain. He subsequently noticed swelling in his left calf, which is tender on examination. His current vital signs reveal a fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C), heart rate 112 bpm, BP 95/65, and an O2 saturation on room air of 91%.
winner_protocol:
Age: 65 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: Acute onset shortness of breath of 30 minutes' duration, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, and an initial feeling of faintness without loss of consciousness, in the setting of recent left total hip replacement and left calf swelling.

Analysis: The patient presents with acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, presyncope, tachycardia (HR 112 bpm), borderline hypotension (BP 95/65), and hypoxemia (O2 saturation 91% on room air) one week after total left hip arthroplasty, followed by 3 days of bed rest for poorly controlled pain. He also has unilateral left calf swelling and tenderness, strongly suggesting deep vein thrombosis (DVT). The combination of recent major orthopedic surgery, immobilization, and unilateral leg swelling satisfies multiple components of Virchow's triad and establishes high pretest probability for venous thromboembolism. The acute respiratory and hemodynamic compromise is most consistent with acute pulmonary embolism (PE) arising from lower extremity DVT, with presyncope, tachycardia, and borderline hypotension indicating possible right ventricular strain and a high-risk (submassive or massive) PE. Differential diagnoses considered include acute coronary syndrome, pneumonia, pneumothorax, aortic dissection, pericarditis, heart failure, and sepsis/DVT-related cellulitis; however, the classic risk factor profile and symptom constellation make PE the most likely diagnosis. The low-grade fever may reflect pulmonary infarction from PE, though surgical site infection or pneumonia should also be considered. Fat embolism syndrome is less likely given the one-week postoperative interval but remains a consideration.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA), 12-lead ECG, chest X-ray, cardiac biomarkers (troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP), bedside echocardiogram to assess right ventricular strain, lower extremity venous Doppler ultrasound, D-dimer, arterial blood gas, blood type and screen, and continuous hemodynamic monitoring equipment.

Conclusion: This is a high-risk acute pulmonary embolism (PE) secondary to deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the left lower extremity, presenting with hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia), hypoxemia, and presyncope suggestive of right heart strain. The patient requires immediate emergent evaluation, stabilization, and treatment in an emergency department or intensive care setting.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Emergency

Recommendations: Initiate supplemental oxygen to maintain adequate oxygenation, establish IV access with continuous hemodynamic monitoring, and obtain urgent CTPA to confirm the diagnosis. Promptly initiate parenteral anticoagulation (unfractionated heparin or LMWH) unless contraindicated, given the recent major surgery and associated bleeding risk. Assess for right ventricular dysfunction via echocardiogram and biomarkers (troponin, BNP) for risk stratification. If massive PE with persistent hypotension or shock develops, consider systemic thrombolysis or embolectomy, weighing the significant bleeding risk from recent total hip arthroplasty; obtain blood type and screen early in case intervention is needed. If anticoagulation is contraindicated, consider IVC filter placement. Admit to an ICU or monitored bed for continuous monitoring. Evaluate for possible surgical site infection or pneumonia given the low-grade fever, and consider fat embolism syndrome as a less likely alternative. Determine the patient's VTE prophylaxis status during the postoperative period, as this is critical and currently unknown.

Notes: The recent major surgery confers a significant bleeding risk that complicates thrombolytic therapy. The low-grade fever may be due to pulmonary infarction rather than infection, but infection should be excluded. VTE prophylaxis status is unknown and should be clarified. Near-syncope suggests transient reduction in cardiac output and supports high-risk PE classification.

Diagnosis10: Premature separation of placenta with coagulation defect

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
